title: Chief Mahue / Mayhew of Unkechaug
summary: Mahue, also written Mahew, Mayhew, or John Mahue, was an Unkechaug and Setauket-connected proprietor, headman, and negotiator in seventeenth-century records. His name appears in land and testimony records that show Native authority, community representation, and diplomacy in the Brookhaven and Moriches area.
content:
Mahue, also written Mahew, Mayhew, or John Mahue, was a seventeenth-century Unkechaug and Setauket-connected proprietor, headman, and negotiator. His name appears in land and testimony records from 1655 through 1691. The cited sources do not establish his birth date and show that he had died by August 1703.

Historical Context

On April 14, 1655, Mahue appears with Warawakmy and other Native signers in the Setauket deed for North Shore land between Stony Brook and the Peconic headwaters.1

In 1659, Mahue appears in the Cataconacke/Old Field deed context, another Setauket-area record of Native land negotiation.1

By December 1685, Mahue was back in the Moriches area, where he sold Governor Thomas Dongan a patent for a large tract of land.1

These records show a leader moving through overlapping Setauket and Unkechaug contexts while facing colonial pressure on community land and authority.1

References

  1. John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History, pp. 41, 80, 82.
  2. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent.
why_this_matters: Mahue shows Unkechaug leadership in land, kinship, and community survival records. His biography connects Setauket, Moriches, Watchogue, and Poospatuck histories without reducing him to a single colonial title.
